title: Collective algorithmic transparency, consultation, and co-determination

observations.claim: The Platform Work Directive requires worker-representative information and consultation before introduction of or substantial changes to automated monitoring or decision systems.
Platform-worker representatives may obtain comprehensive system information and may receive expert assistance for consultation.
limits: National implementation and proportionality conditions remain open.

observations.claim: German Section 87 provides works-council co-determination over technical devices intended to monitor behavior or performance.
German Section 90 requires timely information and consultation on technical systems and work processes, expressly including AI.
The consolidated German Act extends selection-guideline participation to AI and treats expert assistance as necessary when the works council evaluates AI.

Spain requires worker representatives to receive information about parameters, rules and instructions underlying algorithms or AI affecting working conditions, access to work and continued employment.

findings.claim: Collective transparency is different from an individual explanation because representatives can compare patterns, negotiate design and retain institutional memory across cases.
limits: The exact powers vary by jurisdiction.

findings.claim: Counterpower is strongest where worker representatives participate before deployment and can block or condition monitoring rather than only appeal after harm.
limits: No claim that a veto exists in every system or jurisdiction.

findings.claim: Trade-secret or vendor delegation cannot erase the employer-side burden to explain the local rules, parameters and adverse use of the system.
limits: Exact disclosure limits and confidentiality rules remain open.

findings.claim: The protocol should require a representative-facing change ledger before deployment, threshold revision or new data-source use.
